On the other hand, additional validations are unnecessary
because most components in an electric-pump cycle, such as
the thrust chamber, feed line, and pump performance, are the
same as those in a gas generator cycle. Furthermore, additional validations have not been conducted because the actual
performance data supplied from commercial products are
used to estimate the mass of the electric motor and pump
for the specific factors, such as the power density and energy
density.

**3 Results and Discussion**

**3.1** **Design Point**

The reported specifications of a small-sized engine which is
operated at high altitude using a bipropellant showed that the
system generally has a thrust of 400–500 N, a propellant supply pressure of 4–30 bar, and an expansion ratio of 150–400

[3]. In this study, it was assumed that the operational altitude
was approximately 30 km, and the burning time was approximately 600 s as the operating conditions. Table 1 summarizes
the requirements.

**3.2** **Operating Conditions for Performance Analysis**

Table 2 lists the specifications of engine to conduct performance analysis, such as the propellant type and performance
of each component. The propellant type, pipe, valve, and
tank, which are the same components for both systems, were
set identically in the left column of Table 2. Different particulars are indicated in the right column for both systems.

markdown_chunks.section: **Performance Analysis and Mass Estimation of a Small-Sized Liquid** **Rocket Engine with Electric-Pump Cycle** > 123
markdown_chunks.text:
The propellant considered in the study was the LOX/RP1 combination, which is currently being used in most liquid
rocket, and stainless steel 301 was applied to the combustion chamber and nozzle’s material. Stainless steel 301 has a
wide operating temperature range from cryogenic to 1100 K.
Therefore, it shows better performancethanaluminumor carbon fibers under the operating temperature condition of the
engine, and it is used for boosters of large rockets and the
starships project of Space X [28]. The characteristic length
of the combustion chamber is a variable that depends only
on the propellant composition. Generally, 1.02–1.27 m is
recommended for the LOX/RP-1 propellant. In this study,

the characteristic length was set to 1.145 m from the A-1
engine data, which is using the same propellant [29]. In addition, the combustion chamber was assumed to be cylindrical.
The 6061-T6 Aluminum alloy, which is lighter than steel
and maintains robustness even at very low temperatures, was
applied as the material of the propellant tank [28, 30]. The
tank pressure is generally recommended as a specific pressure range depending on the type of propellant. The pressures
of the oxidizer tank and fuel tank were also determined from
the A-1 engine data [29]. The material of the pipe and elbow
was 6061-T6 Aluminum alloy, which is the same as the tank,
for the same reasons. The loss coefficient of the valve was set
by referring to the data of the specific ball valve [31] under
the fully opening condition.

By referring to a previous study [1, 12], the efficiency
of the oxidizer pump, efficiency of the fuel pump, inverter
power density, and the inverter efficiency were set 66%,
61%, 60 kW/kg, and 85%, respectively. The battery structure margin was assumed to be 20%. The battery energy
efficiency is difficult to determine because the specific value
varies according to the discharge time and operating environment conditions. Therefore, the battery energy efficiency
was assumed to be a constant value, which is a logarithmic
function of the final burning time by referring to the energy
efficiency measurement results according to the burning time
of a specific Li-polymer battery of the previous study [1].
The energy efficiency is assumed to be 92.5% from Eq. (38)
because the design burning time was 600 s:

The following three considerations are needed for selecting an electric motor: (1) limitation of the motor output, (2)
rotor heating, and (3) type of motor. The limitation of the
motor output varies according to the type of motor. The motor
output based on the PMSM type was limited to less than a
100 kN thrust [1]. The limitation of motor output has no influence because the required thrust of 500 N in this study was
low enough. In addition, the temperature of the rotor also
increases with increasing thrust. Based on the PMSM type, a
temperature of approximately 390 K and 300 K at a thrust of
100 kN and 10 kN, respectively, were found [1]. At a thrust
of 500 N, it was predicted to be room temperature. Therefore,
motor cooling can be excluded assuming that rotor heating
had no effect.

markdown_chunks.section: **Performance Analysis and Mass Estimation of a Small-Sized Liquid** **Rocket Engine with Electric-Pump Cycle** > 123
markdown_chunks.text:
In general, Li-ion batteries are used mainly in electric
vehicles because of their high power density and energy density. On the other hand, according to the previous study [1], a
large voltage drop was observed within a short discharge time
in an experiment using a specific commercial battery. Therefore, the Li-polymer battery was finally adopted, which is a
candidate for the next-generation batteries. The commercial
battery selected was Amicell’s ABLP8474170H320 model.
Figure 9 shows the detailed performance.

The rotation speed of the turbine, which is a component
of the gas-generator cycle, was applied to 7000 rpm with

reference to the A-1 engine data. The turbine efficiency was
applied to 58.2%, and the maximum inlet temperature limit
of the turbine was set to the melting point of stainless steel
301. Figure 10 shows the design schematics of the electricpump cycle and the gas-generator cycle. Both cycles have a
difference in the components that drive the pump. Moreover,
additional valves to control the flow rate of the gas generator
are present in the gas generator cycle. These additional valves
were modeled using the valve modeling method described in
Sect. 2.1, which is similar to the main valve in the feed line.

**3.3** **Performance Analysis Results**

Performance analysis was conducted for the electricpump cycle and gas generator cycle under the design point
and operating conditions. Table 3 shows the difference in
the mass estimation results for both systems. The tank, feed
line, propellant, and total and dry mass of the electric-pump
cycle were lighter than those of the gas generator cycle. This
was caused by the amount of propellant used to drive the
gas generator because the gas-generator cycle requires more
propellant than the electric-pump cycle under the same conditions, such as thrust and combustion chamber pressure.
